home.heroEyebrow: Understand · Know your options · Get help
home.heroLead: Many government decisions can be reviewed, depending on the law the decision was made under. We cover decisions by the Australian Government (Commonwealth) and the State of Victoria. What Now? turns your letter into plain English, your options into a numbered list, and your next step into a letter — free, no account, your letter is not stored.
home.howStep1Body: Pick the kind of decision, or paste the letter. A few plain questions — no logins.
home.howStep2Body: The review paths open to you, with the official sources we used.
home.howStep3Body: Edit a ready-made draft, or get routed to free help that can take it from here.
home.trust2Body: Every answer shows where it’s from.
home.trust4Body: Real people, when you need them.
home.helpBody: Free help is one tap away — government, tribunals, and community legal centres.
home.helpCta: See the three tiers of help
home.learnTitle: How a decision gets looked at again —
home.learnLead: You can ask the decision-maker to look again, and merits review and judicial review are the two public-law paths after that. Most people have never heard of them. We explain each in plain English: what it is, who hears it, and the grounds of judicial review that people raise. It is free, and built to be easy to follow.
home.linkGroundsDesc: {count} grounds people raise, such as bias and unfairness — in plain English.
home.linkCompareDesc: Which one fits your decision — side by side, with a quick guide.
home.heroNote: the day the letter arrived — start here

home.foilTitle: Find out what you can do
home.foilBody: Three questions, then your review options in order — with every time limit named early and calmly.
home.way1Body: Three questions. Then every pathway, numbered, with time limits.
home.way2Body: Explained clause by clause, in the moment. Your letter is not kept.
home.way3Body: Plain answers, the official source cited beside every one.
home.limitLabel: Time limit — noted early, kept calm
home.limitTitle: We name the time limit early, and calmly.
home.limitBody: Most reviews have a time limit set by the law for your decision. We show the rule and its source — never as a countdown, never in red. There is still time to get help.
home.limitSource: SOURCE: THE ACT FOR YOUR DECISION — NAMED IN YOUR RESULT
home.slotTitle: This slot is empty until we draft it together.
home.slotBody: Answer the three questions and the ready-to-send letter goes here — yours to keep, or to hand to a human service.
home.humansBody: Talk to a person whenever you like — they can take it from here.
home.coverageLead: We cover two governments in detail. If your letter came from either one, you are in the right place. Each one has its own review bodies and its own courts. Whether you can ask for review, and where, depends on the law your decision was made under.
home.covCthBody: Centrelink and Services Australia, child support, the tax office, and other federal agencies. Merits review is at the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART). Judicial review is in the federal courts.
home.covVicBody: Fines and infringements, renting and notices to vacate, public and social housing, councils and state departments. Merits review is at VCAT. A housing decision starts with an appeal to the Housing Appeals Office. A fine can be reviewed by the agency that issued it, or you can elect to have the matter heard in the Magistrates’ Court, which decides the charge rather than reviewing the decision. Judicial review is in the Supreme Court of Victoria.
home.covFoot: In another state? Other states have their own review bodies and their own rules. The guides still explain the ideas, but check the rules where you live — and we always point you to a human service near you.

rights.whoHelp: This helps us find the right review path. Pick the one that fits.
rights.whoVicDesc: A state department, council, or housing office. In another state or territory the steps are much the same, but the rules come from that state's own laws — check them before you rely on a date.
rights.whoCthDesc: Like Centrelink, the tax office, or another federal agency.
rights.whatHelp: Pick the closest one. Each one lists the kinds of decision it covers. If none of these fit, we may not have a guide for your decision — a human service can point you the right way.
rights.dateLabel: What date is on the decision? (optional)
rights.checkHelp: Some of these mean a person should help you directly. Others just mean we will show you how to get help quickly. Leave them blank if none apply.
rights.flagFamily: The decision itself is about child protection, family law, guardianship, or compulsory mental-health treatment
rights.flagCriminal: This decision is connected to a criminal case, a police matter, or a possible prosecution
rights.flagDetention: The decision affects someone who is in prison, immigration detention, or locked care
rights.flagMigration: It is about a visa or migration
rights.flagHearing: A hearing is already booked or underway
rights.flagTribunal: The decision I want to challenge was made by a tribunal, such as VCAT
rights.flagDeadline: The time limit is very soon, or has already passed
rights.consent: I understand this is general information, not legal advice.
rights.routeTitle: Some extra rules apply to your situation
rights.routeBody: What you told us does not stop you working through this. Your options are still below. It does mean some rules are different, and a person can help you with those parts:
rights.goalLead: Tick anything that fits. Most people pick more than one, and that is fine — it helps us put the most useful option first. Nothing here is a commitment.
rights.goal_outcome_desc: You want the debt gone, the payment back, the licence granted, or the notice withdrawn.
rights.goal_lawful: To question how it was made
rights.goal_lawful_desc: You think the process was unfair, or they did not have the power to do it.
rights.goal_information: To find out why, or see the file
rights.goal_information_desc: You want the reasons in writing, or the documents they used.
rights.goal_treatment: To complain about how you were treated
rights.goal_treatment_desc: Delay, rudeness, being ignored, or a process that was not followed.
rights.goal_unsure_desc: That is common. We will show you everything that applies.
rights.goalOtherLabel: Anything else you are hoping for (optional)
rights.goalNote: This orders what we show you. It never hides an option — everything that applies to your decision stays on the next screen.
rights.memoNotAdvice: This is general information, not legal advice. It cannot tell you what will happen in your case. Take it to a human legal service before you rely on it.
rights.memoWhatYouTold: Background — what you have told us
rights.memoIssue1: 1. Eligibility — whether this decision can be taken there, by you, in time
rights.memoIssue1Q: Whether this decision can be taken to this body, by you, and within time.
rights.memoForumIs: For a decision like yours, the body is
rights.memoTimeCheck: Check the time limit for your own decision before you rely on any date. If it has passed, a late application can still be asked for where the law allows it.
rights.memoGroundsLead: Each point below is set out the same way: the question it asks, the rule a court applies, what tends to relate to it, and the answer the other side is likely to give. They are in no particular order, and none of them is a prediction.
rights.memoArgument: What tends to relate to this
rights.memoArgumentNote: Say which of these happened to you, and what you have that shows it.
rights.memoCounter: The answer likely to be given
rights.memoNextBody: These are the options, not a ranking and not a recommendation. You can send an application yourself. You can take these notes to a free legal service, who can tell you which points are worth putting, what evidence you need, and what the time limit is for your own decision. You can do neither, or wait. Nothing here was kept — if you want it, save it now.
rights.memoSourceOfficial: Official source for this kind of decision
rights.avenueMRWhat: A tribunal can look at the decision again and may change it.
rights.avenueJRWhat: A court can check whether the decision was made in a lawful way.
rights.noReview: A formal review may not be available
rights.fallbackNote: We matched this to a general guide. The details of your decision matter, so it is worth checking with a human service.
rights.learnTitle: The ways a decision gets looked at again
rights.learnLead: Before your own options, here is what each one is. They are different things, and they are not all open for every decision. Open whatever is useful — you do not have to read it all. Which of these you can use comes from the law your decision was made under.
rights.learnMore: Read more about how review works
rights.groundsLead: These are the points people raise when asking a court to check that a decision was made lawfully. They are different from what you would tell a tribunal, which looks at your facts and the rules again. They often overlap, so one situation can fit more than one. They are also not the whole list — a lawyer may see points that are not here. Tick anything that sounds like your situation — it will be added to your summary as points to mention. This is general information, not a judgment about your case.
rights.conceptsLead: Questions that come up once you know what went wrong: which body can help, whether you are the right person to ask, and what you can actually walk away with.
rights.reasonsLead: In many cases you can ask the decision-maker, in writing, why they decided the way they did. Whether they must give reasons depends on the type of decision. Here is a draft you can edit and send yourself.
rights.handoffTitle: Take this to a human service
rights.handoffLead: Here is your matter, summarised. It is the same memo as the step before — take it, or read it out. A free service can tell you what it means for your decision, what evidence you need, and what the time limit is. It is your choice whether to go to one.
rights.privacy: Your answers stay on this device. Nothing is stored.
rights.flagFamilyHint: Tick this only if the decision is one of those. If you have a health condition or children, but the decision is about Centrelink, housing, renting or a fine, leave it blank.
rights.urgentTitle: Please call a human service today
rights.urgentBody: You can still read your options below. Bring them to the call — it makes the conversation faster.
rights.analysisLeadBoth: More than one path may be open for this decision. They are listed in the order people usually consider them. Asking the decision-maker to look again is normally the first and the cheapest. Each card below names the body, and says what it decides.
rights.analysisLeadBothConditional: More than one path may be open for this decision, and one of them depends on the law for your decision, or on who made it — the card below says which. They are listed in the order people usually consider them.
rights.analysisLeadMerits: Merits review is open for this decision. A tribunal can look at your case again and make a different decision.
rights.analysisLeadJudicial: Merits review does not appear to be available for this decision. Judicial review asks a court to check that the decision was made lawfully.
rights.analysisLeadNone: A formal review may not be available for this decision. A human service can check that with you, and there may still be other options.
rights.pathConditional: Only if the law for your decision allows it
rights.pathConditionalJudicial: Depends on who made the decision — check this with a free service
rights.pathBodyInternal: This review is done inside the agency, not by a tribunal. Someone there looks at the decision again. Whether a scheme has one at all, who does it, and what they can do with it are set by the Act your decision was made under — so check your decision letter, or ask the agency or a free legal service, before you rely on any of it.
rights.pathBodyMixed: Part of this path is handled inside the agency, not by a tribunal. What an internal reviewer can do with your decision is worth checking with a free legal service. Check which step applies to you.
rights.pathCriteria: What they decide for a decision like yours
rights.focusMerits: The review body is not only asking whether the original officer got it wrong. It looks at the facts again, as they stand now, and decides what the correct or preferable decision is. So what carries weight here is evidence about your situation — documents, dates, letters, and anything that has changed since the decision.
rights.focusJudicial: A court is not deciding whether the outcome was harsh or unfair. It looks at how the decision was made. So what carries weight here is the process — what you were told, what you had a chance to respond to, and what was or was not taken into account. Judicial review starts from a named ground of review.
rights.stepsLead: These are the usual steps people take. You can stop at any point, or hand the whole thing to a human service.
rights.step1: Ask for the reasons in writing
rights.step1Body: Reasons tell you what was taken into account. That is what shows you which path fits, and it helps whichever one you choose. A draft is ready below.
rights.step2Body: Letters, dates, records, and anything that has changed since the decision.
rights.step3: Lodge with {body}, within the time limit
rights.step3Body: The rule for your decision is named above, with its official source.
rights.step4Body: They can check the path, confirm the date, and take it from here if you want them to.
rights.faqLead: Plain-English answers written for this kind of decision.
rights.applyLead: If you decide to go ahead, here is a draft you can edit and send yourself. Pick the path you mean — each letter says something different.
rights.applyMeritsHint: This letter asks a tribunal to look at the decision again on the facts and make the correct or preferable decision.
rights.applyJudicialHint: This letter is about how the decision was made, not the outcome. Judicial review is a court process and it is technical, so this is a starting point to take to a human legal service.
rights.applyNoDraft: There is no draft for this path. Taking a matter to court is a formal step with its own form and its own rules, and we do not hold a checked version of it. Your notes below are ready to take to a free service, who can tell you what to file and by when.

rights.routeAlsoTitle: Other services for this kind of decision
rights.blockedArea: Please choose what the decision is about, above.
rights.blockedConsent: Please tick the box above to continue.

tripwire.familyGuardianshipMentalHealth: Child protection, family law, guardianship and compulsory mental-health decisions run in their own tribunals, with their own rules and often shorter limits. Read on, and take this to a person who works in that area.
tripwire.criminal: There is a criminal side to this. What you write in a review can matter in that case too, so it is worth having a lawyer look at anything before you send it.
tripwire.detention: Someone is being held. Time limits are usually much shorter, and there may be an urgent path. Please call a person today as well as reading on.
tripwire.migration: Visa and migration decisions have their own rules and their own time limits, which are often short. A registered migration agent or lawyer can confirm which apply to you.
tripwire.hearingOnFoot: A hearing is already booked or underway, so timing matters a lot. Please talk to a human legal service today.
tripwire.deadlineImminentOrPassed: Your time limit is very soon, or it has passed. It is sometimes possible to ask for more time, so please contact a human legal service today.
tripwire.privativeClause: This kind of decision has extra rules about going to court. Those rules cannot stop a court checking whether the decision-maker had the power to decide at all. It is technical, so a lawyer should look at it directly.
tripwire.tribunalDecision: A tribunal has already decided, so what is open now is different. There may be an appeal on a point of law, or a court check of how the decision was made. Both have short limits, so please talk to a free legal service this week.

rights.stopStillHelpful: There is still something useful you can do before you call.
rights.stopCallNowNote: You told us this involves a criminal matter or someone being held. Talking to a lawyer today matters more than anything else on this page.
rights.stopPrepLead: Human services are busy. Having these ready makes your call shorter and more useful.
rights.stopPrep1: The letter or notice itself, and the envelope it came in.
rights.stopPrep2: The date on it, and the date you received it.
rights.stopPrep3: Any reference or file number on the letter.
rights.stopPrep4: Anything you have already sent or said to them, and when.
rights.stopPrep5: Names and dates of anyone you have spoken to.
rights.stopPrep6: Whether anyone else is helping you already, such as a caseworker or a support worker.
rights.stopPrepNote: You do not have to write anything down that is hard to write. You can tell the service out loud instead.
rights.stopAskLead: These are questions people find useful to ask a human service.
rights.stopAsk1: Is there a time limit I need to know about, and what is it?
rights.stopAsk2: Can you act for me, or do you give advice only?
rights.stopAsk3: If you cannot help, who else can?
rights.stopAsk4: Is there anything I should not do while I wait?
rights.stopAsk5: What should I bring to an appointment?
rights.stopNotesLead: We can put your answers into a short note to take to a human service. We do not keep a copy. It will save onto this device, so if you share this phone or computer with someone, printing it or writing it out by hand may be safer.
rights.stopNotesArea: The area this tool was set to
rights.stopNotesTicked: What I ticked in the tool
rights.stopNotesAttribution: (Prepared with a free self-help tool, using the answers I gave it. General information only, not legal advice.)
rights.flagCriminalHint: Tick this if police, a prosecutor or a court is involved in this decision in any way, including if you have been asked to attend an interview, or you have been told a debt may be referred.
rights.flagDetentionHint: Tick this if the person this decision is about is being held, or is about to be released.
rights.outOfScope: Some decisions — visas, criminal matters, child protection, family law, guardianship, or compulsory mental-health treatment — carry extra rules and shorter limits. You can still work through this. Tell us below and we will factor it in, and we will point you to a person as well.
rights.accountLead: Write it once, in your own words. There is no right way to say it.
rights.accountPrivacy: What you write stays on this device unless you press the button below.
rights.accountQWant: What do you want to happen now?
rights.accountQChanged: Has anything changed since the decision?
rights.accountQAttach: What can you send with your letter?
rights.accountGroundHint: It might help to think about:
rights.accountGroundNoteLawyer: This one is not in your letter. It goes in your note for a human legal service.
rights.accountGroundNoteSerious: This is a serious thing to say about a person. It is not in your letter or your note. Please raise it with a human legal service.
rights.groundsLeadMerits: These are problems people point to. Tick anything that sounds like your situation. What you tick shapes the letter below, and nothing is decided for you.
rights.accountHint: Useful things to include: what the decision was about, what you told them and when, anything they never asked you about, what has changed since, and what you want to happen now.
rights.accountPlaceholder: Start anywhere. You can come back and add more.
rights.letterBtn: Put my words into the letter
rights.letterSendNote: This one sends what you wrote to us, so we can slot it under the points you marked. We do not keep it.
rights.letterPickLead: These are your own words, put under the points you marked. Tick the ones that are true and that you are happy to send. Anything you leave unticked stays out.
rights.letterCheckTrue: Only tick a line if it is true and you could explain it to someone who asked.
rights.letterSensitive: This line mentions something that can count against you. Think about whether it needs to go in.
rights.letterNothing: We could not find anything in what you wrote that fits the points you marked. Your letter below still works, and you can add your own words to it.
rights.letterThirdParty: It looks like you are writing for someone else. This part only works when the letter is about your own decision. You can still edit the letter below yourself.
rights.letterUnavailable: This is not available right now. Your letter below still works.
rights.flagTribunalHint: Tick this only if a tribunal has already decided. If your letter came from an agency and has not been to a tribunal yet, leave it blank.
rights.groundNotesTitle: What happened, on each point you marked
rights.groundNotesLead: Write what happened in your own words. It goes into your memo under that point, exactly as you write it. Leave any of them blank if you would rather not.
rights.groundNotesPlaceholder: For example: what you were told, when, and by whom.
rights.groundNotesPrivacy: This stays on your device while you write it. It is not sent anywhere from this step.
rights.memoYourNote: What you told us about this point
rights.urgentBanner: From what you ticked, this may not be able to wait. A free service can help you today.
rights.pathTitleNotTribunal: Having the decision looked at again
rights.pathMatchesGoal: Matches what you said you want
rights.pointsNeedPathLead: What you raise depends on which approach you take. A tribunal looks at the facts and the rules again. A court looks at how the decision was made. They are not the same questions.
rights.criteriaTitle: What the tribunal decides for a decision like yours
rights.criteriaLead: These are the questions the tribunal looks at. Tick any that relate to your situation, and say what happened. You do not have to tick them all — only what you have something to say about.
rights.criteriaTitleOther: What this body decides for a decision like yours
rights.criteriaLeadOther: This one is not a tribunal, so what it can do is worth checking with a free service. Tick any point below that relates to your situation, and say what happened.
rights.internalCriteriaTitle: What the reviewer looks at for a decision like yours
rights.internalCriteriaLead: These are the points the reviewing body considers. Tick any that relate to your situation, and say what happened. There is also a box at the end for anything not on the list.
rights.criteriaPlaceholder: What happened, and anything you have that shows it.
rights.reasonsDisclose: Open this if you want to ask the decision-maker to put their reasons in writing.
rights.memoSummaryWants: You said you are hoping for:
rights.memoSummaryPath: The approach worked through here is
rights.memoSummaryOnePoint: It works through one point you marked.
rights.memoSummaryPoints: It works through {n} points you marked.
rights.memoSummaryReads: Three sections follow: eligibility, what that body decides, and the points raised.
rights.focusInternal: This is the decision-maker looking at its own decision again. What carries weight is what they did not have, or did not take into account — documents, dates, and anything that has changed. It is usually free, and it may be quicker than an outside review. The rules differ from one Act to the next, so check what yours says.
rights.focusCourt: This one is a court, and it hears the matter itself rather than reviewing the decision. It can end differently from the decision you have now, including on cost. Free legal help before you take this step is worth having.
rights.internalAskTitle: What you are asking them to look at again
rights.internalAskLead: There is no set list for an internal review — the rules differ by department. Say what you want looked at again, and why. It goes into your memo in your words.
rights.internalAskPlaceholder: For example: what they did not have, or did not take into account.
rights.applyLeadChosen: This draft follows the approach you chose. It is yours to edit and send yourself, and nothing is sent for you.
rights.applyInternalHint: This letter asks the decision-maker to look at its own decision again, and asks what the time limit is for the next step.
rights.memoIssue1Internal: 1. Eligibility — whether an internal review is open to you
rights.memoIssue1QInternal: Whether this decision can be looked at again by the people who made it.
rights.memoIssue2Internal: 2. Scope — what an internal review is, and is not
rights.memoIssue3Internal: 3. What you are asking them to look at
rights.memoInternalBodyIs: For a decision like yours, the people who look again are
rights.memoSummaryReadsInternal: Three sections follow: eligibility, what an internal review is, and what you are asking them to look at.
rights.memoSummaryReadsInternalShort: Two sections follow: eligibility, and what an internal review is.
rights.memoNotATribunal: This body is not a tribunal conducting merits review. What it can do with your decision is not set out here, and a free service can tell you.
rights.pathsAreSequence: For this kind of decision these usually run in order. Most people start at step 1, and the later steps normally follow it. Each step has its own time limit, so check the limit for the step you are on.
rights.pathsAreAlternatives: For this kind of decision these are different choices, not stages. You do not have to do one before another, and choosing one can close another. They are numbered only in the order people usually think about them. A free service can tell you which fits.
rights.pathsAreUnknown: These are numbered in the order people usually consider them. Whether one has to come before another depends on the law for your decision, so check that before you rely on it.
rights.pointsContextTitle: What you have told us so far
rights.pointsContextStory: Read back what you wrote about what happened
rights.pointsWritten: You have written on {n} of the points below. All of it goes into your memo.
rights.criteriaAsk: What happened on this point? Say it in your own words.
rights.nextNeedsStory: Write a little about what happened first. A sentence or two is enough.
rights.nextNeedsGoal: Pick what you are hoping for first. “I am not sure” is a real answer.

rights.memoMorePlaceholder: For example: a letter they sent in June that I never replied to.

privacy.title: Your privacy
privacy.intro: This service is built so that we don't keep your letter or your answers.
privacy.point1: Your letter is read on the spot to explain it, then discarded. We don't store it on our servers and we don't log what it says.
privacy.point2: There's no account and no login. Anything kept for your convenience stays on your own device, and you can clear it any time.
privacy.point3: We don't put your personal details into analytics.
privacy.point4: When you connect with a human legal service, you deal with them directly under their own privacy rules.

about.title: About this service
about.intro: This is a free self-help tool that helps people understand and respond to government decisions.
about.infoNotAdvice: This service gives general information, not legal advice, and cannot tell you what will happen in your case. For advice about your own situation, talk to a human legal service.
about.groundedBody: Every answer is grounded in a checked set of rules and points to where it comes from. When something isn't covered, the service says so and points you to a person who can help — it never guesses.
about.currencyBody: Rules and time limits change. Each entry carries the date it was last checked, and entries are reviewed on a regular cycle.

consent.message: We use privacy-friendly analytics to understand how the service is used. No personal details are collected.

tour.replayDone: Guides reset — open a step to see them
tour.whoOptionsText: This one answer sets your whole path. A federal decision and a state decision are heard by different bodies, so we ask first and then only show you what fits.
tour.privacyText: Your answers stay on your device. There is no login, and we never keep your letter or what you tell us.
tour.areaText: It does not have to be exact. If nothing fits, choose the general option — you will still get the review path and free help.
tour.dateTitle: The date helps, but it is optional
tour.dateText: If you have the letter in front of you, the date on it lets us show timing information that fits your situation.
tour.tripwireText: These are situations where a person, not a self-help tool, should help you. Some mean a person should help you directly. Others just mean we will show you how to get help quickly. Nothing is hidden either way — your options still follow.
tour.consentText: We give general information, not legal advice, and we cannot tell you what will happen in your case. Tick to say you understand, then continue.
tour.avenueText: Asking the decision-maker to look again is usually the first step. A tribunal can look at the decision again and may change it. A court checks whether it was made lawfully — not whether it was a good decision. Only the ones that apply to your decision are shown.
tour.reasonsText: This is a ready-made letter asking the decision-maker to explain their reasons. Copy it, edit anything you like, and send it yourself.
tour.groundsText: Tick anything that resembles what happened to you. It becomes a list of points to raise with a lawyer — it is not a judgement about your case.
tour.handoffText: This makes a short summary of your situation to bring to a human legal service, so you do not have to explain it all from scratch. It is built on your device.
tour.askInputText: Plain language works best — write it as you would say it. There is no need for legal terms.
tour.askSubmitText: We only answer from a checked set of rules, and we show you where each answer came from. If your question is not covered, we say so and point you to someone who can help.
tour.decodeUploadTitle: A photo of the letter is enough
tour.decodeUploadText: Take a picture or upload a PDF. We read it on the spot to explain it, then discard it — the letter is never stored.
tour.decodePasteText: If it is easier, type or paste what the letter says. You do not need the whole thing — the main paragraphs are plenty.
tour.decodePrivacyText: We never keep your letter. Close the tab and nothing about it remains.

install.title: Keep this on your phone
install.body: Add What Now? to your home screen so you can find your way back without hunting for the link. It stays free, and it still keeps no letter.

letter.groundsLead: Below are the things I want looked at. I marked these from a list of common problems. I am not a lawyer.
letter.otherConcerns: I have other concerns about this decision. I am taking those to a human legal service.
letter.groundHearing: I did not get a chance to have my say
letter.groundRelevant: I gave them information the decision does not mention
letter.groundRule: I was told a rule applied, and nobody asked about my situation
letter.groundWrongFact: The decision uses a fact about me that is wrong
letter.groundOffTopic: The reasons talk about something I do not think is part of this decision
letter.groundSigner: The letter names one person as decision-maker, and a different person signed it
